newsitem.title: UK: Russia dominates emerging debt market.
newsitem.headline: Russia dominates emerging debt market.

text.p: The fluctuating fortunes of Russia almost completely overwhelmed the emerging debt market on Friday.

Traders said that with the exception of Russian debt -- which is off from early highs -- there was very little trading in the market and even for Russia, most investors appear to prefer to stay put ahead of the weekend.

Dollar Vneshekonombank paper RUVNUSLNS=RR steamed ahead at the opening, popping above 77 cents in the dollar, some three points above the lows touched on Thursday as fears over Kremlin infighting dragged prices down.
Prices of Russian paper later fell back on some profit-taking and by mid-morning were hovering around a bid of 76-1/2 percent of face value.

Vnesh had initially dropped after Thursday's sacking of security chief Alexander Lebed but, on second thoughts, many traders viewed it as a "lancing of the boil" of the Kremlin feuding which was threatening further political instability.
"On the positive side, it means that the infighting has been dealt with," one European bank trader said.
Several also pointed to relief at seeing a relatively healthy looking Presaident Boris Yeltsin on the televsion announcing Lebed's dismissal.
"But what all this will lead to is anyone's guess," one said, adding it would take time to see whether Lebed would fade away or become an even greater thorn in the side of the administration.
Volatility is likely to remain until investors feel more confident about Yeltsin's health following his heart surgery next month.
"I don't think we're going to see (debt) prices skyrocket at the moment," said Michael Jordan, senior trader at BankAmerica.
By last week, the price had hit 80 cents before political worries and profit-taking took them down.
"There was always going to be a correction, no matter what, and it was just a bit deeper than expected, but prices will ratchet back up," Jordan added.
The rest of the debt market barely moved, though Bulgaria firmed, partly on the back of Russia and what one trader said was a lack of any more bad news out of the country.
Latin American debt is holding relatively steady, helped by firmer U.S. Treasuries.
